# Location Mapping

## Purpose

Turn a designed location into a small coordinate system: named levels, a
fixed left and right, landmarks, exits, and the connections between levels.
Every panel row then states a position as level, side, and landmark, and
`check-continuity.js` can tell when a character has changed level without
climbing anything.

## Use When

- A location file exists and scenes will be staged in the place.
- Blocking or the panel ledger needs a position the map cannot express.
- A review finds a spatial error: a platform on the wrong side, a character
  above when they should be below.
- A new scene uses a part of the location nobody mapped.

## Inputs

- `production/locations/<LOC_ID>/location.yaml`: architecture and named
  structures.
- Scene files that use the location: `cast`, `geography.travel_direction`,
  `geography.threat_direction`, and the action in each beat.
- The existing `production/locations/<LOC_ID>/map.yaml` and the approved
  plate, when there is one.

## Process

1. Fix the viewpoint and the side convention first. Choose the direction
   the reader normally looks from and write `sides.convention` as one
   sentence that names what is on screen left and screen right from there:
   "Bow is screen left, stern is screen right when facing port." Fill
   `left` and `right`. This convention never rotates for the life of the
   project.
2. Choose the convention to suit the action. If the scene's travel runs
   toward the bow and the comic reads left to right, a convention that puts
   the bow on the right lets progress follow the reading direction.
3. Name the levels, bottom to top. Anything a character can stand on at a
   different height is a level: platform and ground, deck and wheelhouse,
   street and balcony. The test is whether someone on one would have to
   climb or drop to reach the other.
4. Place the landmarks. Each has an `id`, a `level`, a `side` (`left`,
   `right`, or `center`), and a `description`. Use the fixed structures from
   `location.yaml`. Every area where action happens needs at least one
   landmark, so that a panel never has to say "somewhere on the left".
5. Record depth in the landmark descriptions. The map has no depth field,
   so write whether each landmark sits near the reader's edge or at the
   back in the default view: "at the far rail", "against the near
   bulwark". Panels use this to separate foreground from background.
6. Settle inside and outside. If the story stages panels in both, the
   interior is its own location and an exit joins the two. If the outside
   is only glimpsed through an opening, a landmark for the opening is
   enough.
7. List the exits: `id`, `level`, `side`, and `leads_to` (a location ID, or
   null). A character who leaves the scene goes through one of them, and a
   threat that arrives comes in by one.
8. List the connections between levels: `from`, `to`, and `via`, where
   `via` is a landmark. A pair of levels with no connection cannot be
   crossed. A character who changes level in the ledger must set `moved`,
   or the panel must declare an `ellipsis`.
9. Walk every scene through the map. For each beat, state each character's
   position as level, side, and landmark. Where the map cannot express a
   position, add the missing landmark now.
10. Compare the map with the plate. Each landmark appears on the side the
    map gives it. When an approved plate and the map disagree, fix the map
    to match the plate or supersede the plate; do not leave both standing.
11. Run `node scripts/validate-workspace.js --root <workspace>` and
    `node scripts/check-continuity.js --root <workspace>`. Both fail on a
    panel that names a level or landmark the map does not have.

## Outputs

- `production/locations/<LOC_ID>/map.yaml` (`location-map` schema): `levels`,
  `sides`, `landmarks`, `exits`, `connections`.

## Quality Bar

- `sides.convention` is one sentence that names a viewpoint and both sides.
- Every landmark's `level` is one of the listed levels.
- Every pair of levels a scene moves between has a connection, and each
  `via` is a landmark.
- Every position used in a page of this location can be written with the
  map's levels, sides, and landmarks.
- Every exit a scene uses is listed, with `leads_to` set where the
  destination is a mapped location.
- The plate and the map agree on which side each landmark is on.

## Common Failure Modes

- No stated convention. The loading platform is on the left on page 2 and
  on the right on page 5, and nothing on file says which is wrong.
- A platform and the ground treated as one level. The character who should
  be firing from above is drawn standing next to the person below.
- Two levels with no connection listed, so a character appears on the upper
  one without any panel showing how.
- Landmarks named after things that move. A crate that gets pushed aside
  stops being a fixed point.
- Inside and outside sharing one map, with a wall the characters seem to
  walk through.
- A convention that changes because one panel looked better from the other
  side. Reverse angles are a framing choice; the map stays where it is.
- Too few landmarks, so every position is "center" and the review has
  nothing to compare against.

## Notes

The map is what `scene-blocking` stages on and what `state-tracking` cites
in every ledger row. A panel drawn from the opposite side still records
positions in map terms and notes the reversed view in its framing. The
rules are `rules/visual/spatial-continuity.md` and
`rules/visual/location-consistency.md`.
